records.our_prose: Across the cold northern tier snow peas are a spring crop, with a second fall crop where the season allows. Sow as soon as the ground can be worked, even weeks before the last frost, since pea seedlings are cold-hardy; the spring crop is harvested in late spring to early summer and then ends as midsummer heat stops the vines and brings on powdery mildew. The hot weeks are left out, and a late-summer sowing gives a fall crop the frost-tolerant plants carry into autumn. From the milder end of the region (zone 7) a fall sowing can be grown through the cool months for a winter-into-spring harvest. The summer gap here is a true heat exclusion for peas, backed at each cell.

records.our_prose: St. George grows snow peas on a single spring, direct-sown cycle, per USU Extension's "Suggested Vegetable Planting Dates for Utah," which sets Feb 15 as the St. George Group A (hardy) date for peas. Pods begin about 62 days later, and the vines are pulled by early May, well ahead of the 100°F heat St. George reaches from June into September. USU's planting-date table documents no fall pea window for the St. George area, unlike the handful of Group E crops (beets, cabbage, kale, lettuce, onion, spinach, turnip) that do get one, so this cell runs a single spring cycle rather than a fabricated second one.
